question: Which connective tissue layer directly surrounds an individual skeletal muscle fascicle?
cited_learning_objective: Recall the hierarchical organization of skeletal muscle as a tissue and identify the endomysium, perimysium, and epimysium.

options.rationale: Perimysium is the dense connective tissue layer that directly encloses a bundle of muscle fibers known as a muscle fascicle.
Endomysium surrounds individual muscle fibers, not an entire fascicle. For this to be correct, the stem would need to ask for the lining of a single cell.
Epimysium surrounds the entire skeletal muscle organ rather than individual fascicles. For this to be correct, the stem would ask about the outermost muscle covering.
The sarcolemma is the plasma membrane of the muscle fiber cell, not a connective tissue layer enclosing fascicles. For this to be correct, the stem would ask for the cell membrane.
Sarcoplasm is the cell cytoplasm, not a connective tissue sheath. For this to be correct, the stem would ask for the intracellular fluid matrix.

question: Which structure consists of two terminal cisternae flanking a single central transverse tubule?
cited_learning_objective: Recall the specialized cellular components of muscle fibers: sarcolemma, sarcoplasm, t-tubules, sarcoplasmic reticulum, triad/dyad, and myofibrils.

options.rationale: A dyad consists of one transverse tubule and a single small sarcoplasmic reticulum element, characteristic of cardiac muscle. For this to be correct, the stem would specify a two-component junction.
In skeletal muscle, a triad is formed by one central T-tubule flanked on either side by two terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum at the A-I junction.
Dense bodies are cytoplasmic attachment sites for thin filaments in smooth muscle. For this to be correct, the stem would describe smooth muscle filament anchoring.
Intercalated discs are intercellular junctional complexes in cardiac muscle. For this to be correct, the stem would ask for cell-to-cell adhesion structures.
Focal adhesions connect smooth muscle myofilaments to the cell membrane/external lamina. For this to be correct, the stem would ask about membrane-bound densities in non-striated muscle.

question: Which region of the sarcomere contains large quantities of bound creatine kinase to regenerate adenosine triphosphate?
cited_learning_objective: Visually identify the features of the sarcomere: A-band, I-band, H-band, Z-line

options.rationale: The Z-line anchors actin thin filaments between adjacent sarcomeres via alpha-actinin. For this to be correct, the stem would ask for the boundary structure of the sarcomere.
The I-band consists exclusively of thin actin filaments. For this to be correct, the stem would ask for the isotropic light band lacking thick filaments.
The M-line located at the center of the sarcomere contains myomesin and large amounts of bound creatine kinase, which functions as an energy shuttle to regenerate ATP.
The A-band represents the total length of thick myosin filaments. For this to be correct, the stem would ask for the broad anisotropic dark band.
The H-zone is the paler region within the A-band lacking thin filaments. For this to be correct, the stem would ask for the zone containing thick filaments only.

question: Which structural component of cardiac muscle contains fascia adherens, desmosomes, and gap junctions?
cited_learning_objective: Compare and contrast the specialized cellular components of skeletal, smooth, and cardiac muscle fibers and describe their functions. Ex.: nuclei, diad/triad, intercalated discs, morphology

options.rationale: Terminal cisternae store calcium ions within muscle cells. For this to be correct, the stem would ask for calcium storage sites.
Triads conduct action potentials into skeletal muscle fibers. For this to be correct, the stem would ask for membrane invaginations in skeletal muscle.
Focal densities anchor thin filaments in smooth muscle cells. For this to be correct, the stem would ask about non-striated muscle anchors.
Intercalated discs join adjacent cardiac muscle cells and comprise fascia adherens (anchoring actin), desmosomes (cytoskeletal anchors), and gap junctions (electrical continuity).
Peripheral nuclear domains describe the location of nuclei in multinucleated skeletal muscle cells. For this to be correct, the stem would ask about skeletal muscle nuclear location.

question: During skeletal muscle contraction, which event directly causes the myosin head to detach from the active actin binding site?
cited_learning_objective: Understand the general process of a skeletal muscle contraction and the sliding filament theory

options.rationale: Calcium binding to troponin exposes the active site on actin. For this to be correct, the stem would ask what initiates cross-bridge formation.

options.text: Release of inorganic phosphate from myosin
options.rationale: Release of inorganic phosphate and ADP drives the myosin power stroke. For this to be correct, the stem would ask what powers the bending of the myosin head.

options.text: Hydrolysis of ATP into adenosine diphosphate
options.rationale: ATP hydrolysis recocks the myosin head into a high-energy state after detachment has already occurred. For this to be correct, the stem would ask how myosin returns to its cocked position.

options.text: Depolarization extending along the transverse tubule
options.rationale: T-tubule depolarization triggers calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. For this to be correct, the stem would ask how electrical signals enter the cell depth.

options.text: Attachment of new adenosine triphosphate molecule
options.rationale: Binding of a new ATP molecule to the myosin head causes conformational changes that release the cross-bridge from actin.

question: When a skeletal muscle fiber transitions from a relaxed state to a fully contracted state, which sarcomere measurement remains unchanged?
cited_learning_objective: Visually identify the features of the sarcomere: A-band, I-band, H-band, Z-line

options.text: Width of the dark A band
options.rationale: The A-band corresponds to the full length of myosin thick filaments, which do not shorten during contraction according to sliding filament theory.

options.text: Width of the pale I band
options.rationale: The I-band shortens/recedes as thin filaments slide deeper into the A-band toward the M-line during contraction.

options.text: Width of the central H zone
options.rationale: The H-zone narrows and disappears as actin filaments slide into the central region of the sarcomere.

options.text: Distance between two adjacent Z discs
options.rationale: The Z-discs move closer together during contraction, defining the overall shortening of the sarcomere.

options.text: Distance between two adjacent M lines
options.rationale: The distance between M-lines of adjacent sarcomeres in series decreases during active shortening.

question: In smooth muscle cells, which structures serve as cytoplasmic anchors for thin filaments, serving a function analogous to Z-discs in striated muscle?
cited_learning_objective: Recall the arrangement of contractile elements in smooth muscle and the way smooth muscle functions.

options.rationale: Corbular SR is a specialized sarcoplasmic reticulum component in cardiac myocytes. For this to be correct, the stem would ask about cardiac intracellular calcium stores.
Dense bodies (focal densities) in smooth muscle cytoplasm anchor actin thin filaments, serving the same structural anchoring role as Z-discs in striated muscle.
Caveolae are plasma membrane invaginations in smooth muscle involved in ion transport and signal transduction. For this to be correct, the stem would ask for membrane invaginations.
Gap junctions transmit electrical excitation between adjacent smooth muscle cells. For this to be correct, the stem would ask for electrical coupling sites.
Fascia adherens junctions anchor actin filaments at cardiac intercalated discs. For this to be correct, the stem would specify cardiac muscle cell-to-cell anchoring.

question: Which cell type resides around capillaries and venules, regulates vascular lumen diameter, and possesses mesenchymal stem cell potential during injury?
cited_learning_objective: Recall the function and location of skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle cells and recognize them by their microscopic appearance

options.rationale: Myoepithelial cells are contractile cells surrounding exocrine gland acini. For this to be correct, the stem would specify salivary, sweat, or mammary glands.
Myofibroblasts produce collagen and contract wound sites during tissue fibrosis. For this to be correct, the stem would describe scar tissue formation.
Pericytes wrap around capillaries and venules to control blood vessel diameter and can act as mesenchymal stem cells for tissue repair and angiogenesis.
Myoblasts are precursor cells that fuse to form multinucleated muscle fibers during development. For this to be correct, the stem would describe muscle development.
Satellite cells reside beneath the basal lamina of mature skeletal muscle fibers for muscle regeneration. For this to be correct, the stem would specify muscle fiber repair.

question: Transmission electron microscopy of a cardiac muscle specimen reveals an abundance of an organelle occupying nearly 40% of the cytoplasmic volume. Which organelle is described?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize organelles on stained slides and electron micrographs. Specifically: nuclei, mitochondria, sarcoplasmic reticulum, t-tubules

options.rationale: Sarcoplasmic reticulum is present but less extensive in cardiac muscle compared to skeletal muscle. For this to be correct, the stem would ask about calcium storage membranes.
T-tubules are invaginations of the sarcolemma, not membrane-bound organelles taking up 40% of cytoplasm. For this to be correct, the stem would ask for membrane conduits.
Glycogen granules are associated with energy storage but do not constitute 40% of cardiac cell volume. For this to be correct, the stem would ask for electron-dense nutrient granules.
Mitochondria account for roughly 40% of the cytoplasmic volume in cardiomyocytes to sustain continuous aerobic energy generation.
Nuclei occupy a minor central volume within cardiomyocytes. For this to be correct, the stem would describe central genetic storage structures.

question: A microscopic section shows non-striated, spindle-shaped cells with single, centrally located, elongated nuclei featuring blunt ends. Which tissue is present?
cited_learning_objective: Compare and contrast the specialized cellular components of skeletal, smooth, and cardiac muscle fibers and describe their functions. Ex.: nuclei, diad/triad, intercalated discs, morphology

options.rationale: Skeletal muscle fibers are striated and feature multiple peripherally located nuclei. For this to be correct, the stem would describe peripheral multinucleation.
Cardiac myocytes are striated and branching, typically containing 1-2 central rounded nuclei with intercalated discs. For this to be correct, the stem would specify intercalated discs.
Myotubes are developing multinucleated cells with central rows of multiple nuclei. For this to be correct, the stem would describe multiple centrally aligned nuclei in series.
Purkinje fibers are modified, pale-staining cardiac muscle cells. For this to be correct, the stem would describe enlarged, pale cardiac fibers.
Smooth muscle cells are non-striated, fusiform (spindle-shaped) cells containing a single centrally placed, elongated nucleus with blunt ('cigar-shaped') ends.

question: Which motor protein isoform utilizes ATP hydrolysis to power sliding movements along actin thin filaments rather than tubulin microtubules?
cited_learning_objective: Understand the general process of a skeletal muscle contraction and the sliding filament theory

options.rationale: Myosin is the motor protein that binds and walks along actin thin filaments in contractile cells via ATP-powered cycling.
Kinesin moves intracellular cargo along tubulin microtubules toward the plus end. For this to be correct, the stem would ask for microtubule anterograde transport.
Dynein moves along tubulin microtubules toward the minus end. For this to be correct, the stem would ask for microtubule retrograde transport.
Alpha-tubulin is a structural component of microtubules, not a motor protein. For this to be correct, the stem would ask for a structural subunit.
Protofilaments are polymer tracks composed of tubulin dimers. For this to be correct, the stem would ask for the track rather than the motor protein.

question: Microscopic examination of a mammary gland biopsy demonstrates contractile cells surrounding secretory acini located within the basal lamina. Which cell type is observed?
cited_learning_objective: Recall the function and location of skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle cells and recognize them by their microscopic appearance

options.rationale: Pericytes surround capillaries and venules. For this to be correct, the stem would specify microvascular walls.
Myoepithelial cells are specialized epithelial cells with smooth muscle-like contractile elements found in exocrine glands (sweat, salivary, lacrimal, mammary).
Myofibroblasts reside in interstitial connective tissue during wound healing and fibrosis. For this to be correct, the stem would specify connective tissue repair.
Satellite cells reside in skeletal muscle fibers for muscle regeneration. For this to be correct, the stem would specify skeletal muscle tissue.
Smooth muscle forms distinct muscular layers in hollow visceral organs. For this to be correct, the stem would describe layers within hollow organ walls.

question: In skeletal muscle tissue, at which specific anatomical landmark do transverse tubules extend invaginations into the muscle cytoplasm around myofibrils?
cited_learning_objective: Recall the specialized cellular components of muscle fibers: sarcolemma, sarcoplasm, t-tubules, sarcoplasmic reticulum, triad/dyad, and myofibrils.

options.rationale: T-tubules in cardiac muscle are located near the Z-line, but in skeletal muscle they are at the A-I junction. For this to be correct, the stem would ask for cardiac T-tubule location.
The H-band is in the middle of the A-band and lacks T-tubule invaginations. For this to be correct, the stem would describe thick filament-only zones.
In skeletal muscle, T-tubules invaginate at the boundary junction between the A-band and I-band, forming triads with sarcoplasmic reticulum terminal cisternae.
The M-line is the central attachment line for myosin filaments. For this to be correct, the stem would ask for the center of the sarcomere.
While T-tubules continuous with the sarcolemma originate here, their specific intra-sarcomeric invagination target is the A-I junction. For this to be correct, the stem would ask for origin site.

question: During embryonic development of skeletal muscle, which cellular event directly results in the formation of multinucleated myotubes?
cited_learning_objective: Recall the hierarchical organization of skeletal muscle as a tissue and identify the endomysium, perimysium, and epimysium.

options.rationale: Satellite cell activation occurs during adult regeneration rather than initial embryonic syncytial formation. For this to be correct, the stem would describe adult repair.
Mitosis increases the population of mononuclear myoblasts prior to fusion. For this to be correct, the stem would ask how precursor cell counts expand.
Cardiac fibers undergo branching, but skeletal muscle fibers do not branch and originate from myoblasts. For this to be correct, the stem would specify myocardium.
Mononuclear myoblast precursor cells align end-to-end and fuse together during embryogenesis to create multinucleated myotubes.
Pericytes belong to microvascular walls rather than directly fusing into embryonic skeletal myotubes. For this to be correct, the stem would ask about blood vessel formation.

question: Vascular smooth muscle maintains prolonged structural tone without fatigue through a mechanism allowing cross-bridge retention without continuous ATP consumption. What is this state?
cited_learning_objective: Recall the arrangement of contractile elements in smooth muscle and the way smooth muscle functions.

options.rationale: Rigor mortis is post-mortem rigidity caused by complete ATP depletion in dead tissue. For this to be correct, the stem would describe post-mortem stiffening.
Tetanic contraction is sustained skeletal muscle tension from high-frequency stimulation. For this to be correct, the stem would describe rapid skeletal stimulation.
Phasic contractions are rhythmic, cyclic contractions seen in GI tract smooth muscle. For this to be correct, the stem would describe GI wave movements.
Syncytial contraction refers to wave-like depolarization spreading via gap junctions. For this to be correct, the stem would describe gap junction signaling.
Tonic smooth muscle utilizes a 'latch state' where myosin remains attached to actin 'at rest', holding tension and position without consuming additional ATP.

question: A 45-year-old man is found deceased in his home. Forensic evaluation reveals rigid, fixed limb posture consistent with rigor mortis. What intracellular condition directly causes this finding?
cited_learning_objective: Understand the general process of a skeletal muscle contraction and the sliding filament theory

options.text: Absence of cellular adenosine triphosphate preventing cross-bridge detachment
options.rationale: After death, ATP production stops; without new ATP binding to the myosin head, cross-bridges between actin and myosin cannot detach, locking muscles in rigor mortis.

options.text: Persistent elevation of sarcoplasmic calcium driving continuous power strokes
options.rationale: Power strokes require ATP hydrolysis, which ceases post-mortem; calcium alone cannot drive repeated strokes without ATP. For this to be correct, active power stroke cycling would occur.

options.text: Complete breakdown of actin thin filaments within the I band
options.rationale: Filament degradation occurs later during autolysis, reversing rigor mortis. For this to be correct, the stem would describe loss of muscle rigidity over time.

options.text: Irreversible phosphorylation of myosin light chains at the M line
options.rationale: Myosin light chain phosphorylation regulates smooth muscle rather than post-mortem skeletal muscle rigidity. For this to be correct, the stem would ask about smooth muscle regulation.

options.text: Depleted glycogen storage preventing sodium channel opening along T-tubules
options.rationale: Glycogen depletion limits ATP regeneration, but the immediate cause of cross-bridge locking is the lack of ATP itself. For this to be correct, the stem would ask for pre-mortem metabolic depletion.

question: A 58-year-old man with a long history of alcohol use disorder presents with abdominal distension and jaundice. Liver biopsy shows extensive collagen deposition and tissue contraction driven by transformed mesenchymal cells. Which cell type is responsible for this fibrotic contraction?
cited_learning_objective: Recall the function and location of skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle cells and recognize them by their microscopic appearance

options.rationale: Pericytes surround microvessels to regulate lumen diameter, though they do not drive tissue-wide fibrotic scar contraction. For this to be correct, the stem would focus on capillary regulation.
Myofibroblasts proliferate and differentiate from mesenchymal cells in response to tissue injury, secreting collagen and contracting to pull tissue together; they drive fibrosis in cirrhosis.
Myoepithelial cells reside in exocrine glands to expel secretions. For this to be correct, the stem would describe exocrine gland function.
Satellite cells reside in skeletal muscle fibers to regenerate muscle tissue. For this to be correct, the stem would describe skeletal muscle injury.
Myoblasts fuse during embryogenesis to form myotubes. For this to be correct, the stem would describe developmental muscle formation.

question: A researcher generates a gene mutation in model mice that selectively abolishes the elastic protein titin within skeletal muscle fibers. Which structural alteration will electron microscopy demonstrate?
cited_learning_objective: Visually identify the features of the sarcomere: A-band, I-band, H-band, Z-line

options.text: Complete absence of thin filaments from the pale I band
options.rationale: Thin filaments are composed of actin, tropomyosin, and troponin, not titin. For this to be correct, actin synthesis would be disrupted.

options.text: Disruption of fascia adherens junctions at the intercalated disc
options.rationale: Fascia adherens joins actin filaments across cardiac cells at intercalated discs, not titin in skeletal muscle. For this to be correct, the stem would specify cardiac adhesion.

options.text: Loss of thick filament alignment relative to the Z-line
options.rationale: Titin (connectin) is an elastic protein that anchors thick filaments to the Z-line, keeping the thick filament lattice in register within the sarcomere.

options.text: Inability of transverse tubules to invaginate into the sarcoplasm
options.rationale: T-tubules are invaginations of the sarcolemma lipid bilayer, independent of titin. For this to be correct, the stem would describe sarcolemmal defects.

options.text: Failure of terminal cisternae to store intracellular sarcoplasmic calcium
options.rationale: Calcium storage is handled by sarcoplasmic reticulum proteins (e.g., calsequestrin), not titin. For this to be correct, the stem would focus on SR ion transport.

question: A 62-year-old woman experiences severe cardiac arrhythmia. Electrophysiological testing reveals disrupted cell-to-cell action potential propagation across ventricular myocytes. Which component of the intercalated disc is damaged?
cited_learning_objective: Compare and contrast the specialized cellular components of skeletal, smooth, and cardiac muscle fibers and describe their functions. Ex.: nuclei, diad/triad, intercalated discs, morphology

options.rationale: Fascia adherens mechanically anchors terminal actin filaments between cardiomyocytes. For this to be correct, the stem would describe physical cell detachment during contraction.
Desmosomes provide mechanical anchoring for intermediate filaments. For this to be correct, the stem would describe mechanical tensile weakness.
Terminal cisternae store intracellular calcium rather than propagating intercellular electrical currents. For this to be correct, the stem would specify intracellular calcium release.
Gap junctions within intercalated discs provide low ionic electrical resistance, enabling rapid electrical wave propagation so cardiac myocytes contract as a syncytium.

Triads are present in skeletal muscle (dyads in cardiac) and propagate action potentials intracellularly rather than between cells. For this to be correct, the stem would ask for intracellular coupling.

question: An experimental toxin selectively inhibits voltage-gated dihydropyridine receptors located in skeletal muscle sarcolemmal extensions. Which immediate downstream process is blocked?
cited_learning_objective: Recall the specialized cellular components of muscle fibers: sarcolemma, sarcoplasm, t-tubules, sarcoplasmic reticulum, triad/dyad, and myofibrils.

options.text: Attachment of motor neuron axons to the motor endplate
options.rationale: Motor neuron axon attachment occurs presynaptically/neuromuscularly before sarcolemmal signal propagation. For this to be correct, the stem would describe presynaptic nerve terminal pathology.

options.text: Hydrolysis of ATP molecules by the myosin head domain
options.rationale: ATP hydrolysis occurs downstream at the myosin head once active sites are exposed. For this to be correct, the stem would ask about enzymatic cross-bridge cycling.

options.text: Polymerization of intracellular actin monomer chains during cross-bridge formation
options.rationale: Actin filaments are pre-assembled structural polymers, not synthesized on demand by depolarization. For this to be correct, the stem would ask about thin filament formation.

options.text: Binding of acetylcholine neurotransmitters to post-synaptic motor end plates
options.rationale: Acetylcholine binding occurs at the neuromuscular junction prior to T-tubule depolarization. For this to be correct, the stem would describe synaptic receptor blockage.

options.text: Calcium release from terminal cisternae into the surrounding sarcoplasm
options.rationale: Depolarization along T-tubules activates voltage-sensing dihydropyridine (DHP) receptors, which mechanically trigger ryanodine receptors (RyR) on terminal cisternae to release stored calcium.

question: A 24-year-old athlete suffers a severe quadriceps strain during heavy resistance training. Two weeks later, histological analysis shows active skeletal muscle repair and new muscle fiber formation. Which cell type proliferated to restore the tissue?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize organelles on stained slides and electron micrographs. Specifically: nuclei, mitochondria, sarcoplasmic reticulum, t-tubules

options.rationale: Satellite cells are quiescent stem cells located in skeletal muscle tissue beneath the basal lamina that proliferate and differentiate following injury to repair muscle damage.
Pericytes control capillary diameter and vessel repair rather than directly forming new skeletal muscle fibers. For this to be correct, the stem would specify capillary repair.
Myofibroblasts produce connective tissue scar matrix (collagen) rather than new skeletal muscle fibers. For this to be correct, the stem would describe fibrous scar formation.
Myoepithelial cells reside in exocrine glands to compress glandular acini. For this to be correct, the stem would describe exocrine gland tissue.

Myotubes are intermediate fused structures formed by proliferating satellite/myoblast progeny during regeneration, not the original stem cell source. For this to be correct, the stem would ask for the precursor stage.

question: A 35-year-old man undergoes an endoscopy that demonstrates rhythmic, wave-like contractions along the wall of the esophagus and stomach pushing food forward. Which functional class of muscle tissue powers this movement?
cited_learning_objective: Recall the arrangement of contractile elements in smooth muscle and the way smooth muscle functions.

options.rationale: GI peristalsis is involuntary and managed by the autonomic nervous system. For this to be correct, the stem would specify somatically controlled movement.
Phasic smooth muscle contracts rhythmically to produce wave-like movements such as peristalsis along the gastrointestinal tract.

Tonic smooth muscle maintains continuous, long-term contraction without tiring (e.g., vascular walls and sphincters). For this to be correct, the stem would describe sphincter closure or blood vessel tone.
Cardiac muscle is restricted to the myocardium of the heart. For this to be correct, the stem would describe heart contractions.
Skeletal muscle provides voluntary movement of the skeleton (except upper esophagus/sphincters). For this to be correct, the stem would specify voluntary somatic limb motion.

question: A laboratory drug selectively binds troponin C, preventing calcium binding. What is the cellular consequence during skeletal muscle stimulation?
cited_learning_objective: Understand the general process of a skeletal muscle contraction and the sliding filament theory

options.text: Tropomyosin shifts into the groove exposing active actin sites
options.rationale: Tropomyosin shifts only after calcium binds troponin C. Blocking calcium binding prevents this shift. For this to be correct, calcium would successfully bind troponin.

options.text: Myosin heads unbind ATP and undergo an immediate powerstroke
options.rationale: Power strokes require cross-bridge binding to exposed actin sites, which remains blocked. For this to be correct, active actin sites would need to be exposed.

options.text: Tropomyosin remains positioned covering active sites on actin filaments
options.rationale: Without calcium binding to troponin C, troponin cannot undergo the conformational change that moves tropomyosin away from actin's myosin-binding active sites.

options.text: Sarcoplasmic reticulum terminal cisternae fail to reuptake cytosolic calcium
options.rationale: Calcium reuptake is mediated by ATP-driven SERCA pumps, independent of troponin C binding. For this to be correct, the stem would describe SERCA pump inhibition.

options.text: Action potentials fail to propagate along sarcolemmal transverse tubules
options.rationale: T-tubule action potential propagation depends on voltage-gated sodium channels, occurring upstream of troponin. For this to be correct, the stem would describe sodium channel blockage.

question: A muscle biopsy specimen demonstrates a delicate layer of connective tissue directly enveloping an individual skeletal muscle cell, containing small capillary loops that supply blood to that specific cell. Which layer is described?
cited_learning_objective: Recall the hierarchical organization of skeletal muscle as a tissue and identify the endomysium, perimysium, and epimysium.

options.rationale: Epimysium envelops the entire muscle organ. For this to be correct, the stem would describe the sheath covering the entire muscle body.
Perimysium surrounds muscle fascicles (groups of fibers). For this to be correct, the stem would describe enveloping a bundle of fibers.
Deep fascia overlies the epimysium to separate distinct muscle groups. For this to be correct, the stem would describe compartmental fascia separating muscles.
Endomysium is the innermost delicate connective tissue layer that immediately invests each individual muscle fiber (cell) and houses rich capillary networks.
The sarcolemma is the lipid bilayer cell membrane, not the extracellular connective tissue matrix housing capillaries. For this to be correct, the stem would ask for the plasmalemma.

question: Electron microscopy of a myocardial biopsy shows T-tubules associated with a single small sarcoplasmic reticulum element forming dyads, accompanied by central nuclei and branching fibers. Which feature distinguishes this tissue from skeletal muscle?
cited_learning_objective: Compare and contrast the specialized cellular components of skeletal, smooth, and cardiac muscle fibers and describe their functions. Ex.: nuclei, diad/triad, intercalated discs, morphology

options.rationale: Both skeletal and cardiac muscle are striated tissues containing organized sarcomeres. For this to be correct, the stem would describe smooth muscle.
Multiple peripheral nuclei are characteristic of skeletal muscle, whereas cardiac cells have 1-2 central nuclei. For this to be correct, the stem would describe skeletal muscle histology.
Triads (1 T-tubule + 2 terminal cisternae) are specific to skeletal muscle. For this to be correct, the stem would ask for skeletal muscle couplings.
Skeletal muscle is under voluntary somatic control, whereas cardiac muscle is involuntary and autorhythmic. For this to be correct, the stem would describe skeletal motor innervation.
Cardiac muscle features dyads (1 T-tubule associated with 1 small SR component) at the A-I overlap, whereas skeletal muscle features triads (1 T-tubule with 2 terminal cisternae).

question: A researcher performs transverse TEM sectioning across a relaxed skeletal muscle sarcomere and observes a region containing exclusively thick filaments without any thin filaments present. Which sarcomere zone was sectioned?
cited_learning_objective: Visually identify the features of the sarcomere: A-band, I-band, H-band, Z-line

options.rationale: The H-band (H-zone) is the central region of the A-band that contains only thick filaments and lacks overlapping thin filaments in a relaxed sarcomere.
The I-band contains exclusively thin filaments (actin). For this to be correct, the section would show only thin filaments.
The Z-disc contains protein complexes binding thin filaments going in two directions. For this to be correct, the section would show dense actin-anchoring lattice.
The outer regions of the A-band contain overlapping thick and thin filaments in a 1:6 ratio. For this to be correct, the section would show both thick and thin filaments.
The M-line contains cross-linking myomesin proteins and creatine kinase at the center of the H-zone. For this to be correct, the stem would describe M-line protein cross-links.

question: An animal genetics laboratory generates a knockout mouse strain resulting in marked skeletal muscle hypertrophy and hyperplastic muscular enlargement compared to wild-type controls. Deficiency of which regulatory protein accounts for this phenotype?
cited_learning_objective: Recall the function and location of skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle cells and recognize them by their microscopic appearance

options.rationale: Titin is a structural elastic protein maintaining filament alignment; its loss causes myofibrillar breakdown rather than hypertrophy. For this to be correct, muscle degeneration would occur.
Myostatin is a negative regulator of muscle growth; knocking out the myostatin gene produces a 'double muscle' phenotype characterized by muscle hypertrophy and hyperplasia.
Dystrophin links the cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix; loss causes muscular dystrophy/degeneration. For this to be correct, the stem would describe muscle dystrophy.
Actin is essential for thin filament assembly; loss would prevent muscle contraction entirely. For this to be correct, thin filaments would fail to form.
Creatine kinase regenerates ATP at the M-line; its absence impairs rapid ATP buffering rather than causing double-muscling. For this to be correct, ATP regeneration would fail.

question: High-magnification TEM of human skeletal muscle demonstrates small, electron-dense osmiophilic granules located in the subsarcolemmal space and between myofibrils. What is the metabolic function of these structures?
cited_learning_objective: Recognize organelles on stained slides and electron micrographs. Specifically: nuclei, mitochondria, sarcoplasmic reticulum, t-tubules

options.rationale: Calcium is sequestered within the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane system. For this to be correct, the stem would specify sarcoplasmic reticulum cisternae.

options.text: Protein synthesis for thick filament repair
options.rationale: Protein synthesis occurs via polyribosomes/RER, not glycogen granules. For this to be correct, the stem would describe ribosomes or rough ER.

options.text: Glucose storage for rapid energy production
options.rationale: Glycogen granules (subsarcolemmal, intermyofibrillar, intramyofibrillar) appear as electron-dense dots on TEM and store polymerised glucose for local ATP synthesis.

options.text: Phospholipid synthesis for sarcolemmal membrane repair
options.rationale: Phospholipid synthesis occurs in smooth endoplasmic reticulum membranes. For this to be correct, the stem would describe smooth ER tubules.

options.text: Electron transport for oxidative ATP generation
options.rationale: Oxidative phosphorylation occurs within cristae-bearing mitochondria. For this to be correct, the stem would describe double-membrane organelles.

question: A physiological experiment measures intracellular calcium spikes during muscle activation. Which organelle compartment serves as the primary storage site from which calcium is released into the sarcoplasm?
cited_learning_objective: Recall the specialized cellular components of muscle fibers: sarcolemma, sarcoplasm, t-tubules, sarcoplasmic reticulum, triad/dyad, and myofibrils.

options.rationale: T-tubules are extracellular continuations conducting action potentials, not intracellular calcium storage reservoirs. For this to be correct, the stem would ask for extracellular signal conduits.
Caveolae are surface microdomains in smooth muscle, not the primary SR storage site in skeletal fibers. For this to be correct, the stem would specify smooth muscle surface vesicles.
Gap junctions allow direct cell-to-cell ion passage, not internal sarcoplasmic calcium sequestration. For this to be correct, the stem would ask for intercellular channels.
Terminal cisternae are enlarged specialized regions of the sarcoplasmic reticulum (smooth ER) that store concentrated calcium for excitation-contraction coupling.
Z-discs anchor actin thin filaments and do not store calcium ions. For this to be correct, the stem would ask for thin filament structural anchors.

question: Histological examination of contracted arterial smooth muscle cells reveals a dramatic conformational shift in individual cell morphology compared to their relaxed state. Which morphological change occurs during contraction?
cited_learning_objective: Recall the arrangement of contractile elements in smooth muscle and the way smooth muscle functions.

options.text: Transformation from globular to elongated spindle shape
options.rationale: Smooth muscle cells are elongated/fusiform at rest and shorten during contraction. For this to be correct, the stem would describe relaxation.

options.text: Elongation along the long longitudinal cell axis
options.rationale: Contraction causes shortening, not elongation, along the long axis. For this to be correct, the stem would describe passive stretching.

options.text: Formation of multinucleated syncytial skeletal muscle fibers
options.rationale: Smooth muscle cells remain individual mononuclear cells and do not fuse into multinucleated fibers. For this to be correct, the stem would describe myoblast fusion.

options.text: Disassembly of cytoplasmic actin thin filament networks
options.rationale: Actin networks remain intact during sliding filament contraction; they pull on focal densities to shorten the cell. For this to be correct, the stem would describe filament breakdown.

options.text: Transition from elongated spindle to globular shape
options.rationale: Because contractile myofilament bundles crisscross smooth muscle cells and anchor to cytoplasmic dense bodies and membrane focal densities, contraction pulls the cell from an elongated fusiform shape into a globular shape.
